flawed_step: The central step can't be justified: that a Hamiltonian cycle in every vertex neighbourhood can be combined into one Hamiltonian cycle through the whole graph. Nothing in the definition links the local cycles to each other, and the graph need not even be connected. The special case also fails: some maximal planar graphs are not Hamiltonian.
counterexample: (1) Two disjoint copies of K4. Each vertex's neighbourhood is a K3, which has a Hamiltonian cycle, so the graph is locally Hamiltonian. The graph is disconnected, so it has no Hamiltonian cycle. (2) A connected, planar counterexample is the Goldner–Harary graph. Start with the triangular bipyramid: triangle a,b,c plus poles p and q, giving 6 triangular faces. Put a new degree-3 vertex inside each face and join it to that face's 3 corners. This gives a maximal planar graph with 11 vertices. It is locally Hamiltonian, because in a triangulation with at least 4 vertices each vertex's link is a cycle through its whole neighbourhood. The 6 new vertices are pairwise non-adjacent. In an 11-vertex Hamiltonian cycle, those 6 vertices would need at least 6 other vertices between them, but only 5 original vertices exist. So there is no Hamiltonian cycle.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A proof attempt stops at its first step: nothing lets you build a global Hamiltonian cycle out of the local ones. Two disjoint copies of K4 are locally Hamiltonian but not Hamiltonian. The Goldner–Harary graph is a maximal planar, locally Hamiltonian graph with no Hamiltonian cycle: its 6 pairwise non-adjacent degree-3 vertices cannot fit into an 11-cycle with only 5 other vertices.
